definitions.meaning: The 0 to 14 scale that measures acidity and alkalinity: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline, and each step is ten times stronger.
A substance that releases hydrogen ions, H+, when dissolved in water. Acids have a pH below 7.
A substance that releases hydroxide ions, OH-, when dissolved in water. Alkalis have a pH above 7 and are soluble bases.
A hydrogen ion released by an acid in water. The more H+ ions in excess, the lower the pH.
A hydroxide ion released by an alkali in water. The more OH- ions in excess, the higher the pH.
The reaction of an acid with an alkali, in which H+ and OH- ions pair up to form water and the leftover ions form a salt.
The ionic compound left over after neutralisation. Its second name comes from the acid: chloride, nitrate or sulfate.
A dye that changes colour in acid and alkali, used to test pH. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali.
Adding a solution drop by drop from a burette to find exactly how much is needed to neutralise the other solution.
The point in a titration where the acid and alkali have exactly reacted, shown by the vertical jump on the pH curve.
An acid that only partly releases its hydrogen ions in water, such as the acid in vinegar. It is still acidic, just not strong.

mechanismSteps: Acids and alkalis around you - lemon juice and vinegar are acids, soap and baking soda are alkalis, and chemists sort them all on the pH scale.
The pH scale ladder - the scale runs from 0 to 14 with 7 neutral, and each step away from 7 is ten times stronger.
What pH is really about: ions - acids release H+ ions and alkalis release OH- ions in water, and whichever ion is in excess decides the pH.
Neutralisation: a worked example - H+ and OH- ions pair up to make water, and the leftover ions form a salt: acid plus alkali gives salt plus water.
The litmus test - blue litmus turns red in acid and red litmus turns blue in alkali; no change means neutral.
Naming the salt - hydrochloric acid gives a chloride, nitric acid a nitrate, and sulfuric acid a sulfate.
A common mistake: all acids are strong - a weak acid only partly releases its hydrogen ions, so vinegar is acidic without being strong.
The titration curve: watch for the jump - base added drop by drop moves the pH slowly, then one drop leaps it from 4 to 10 at the equivalence point, where the indicator must change colour.
objectives: Read the pH scale and classify a solution as acidic, neutral or alkaline
Explain acidity and alkalinity in terms of H+ and OH- ions
Describe neutralisation, name salts from their acids, and read the jump on a titration curve
subject: science
title: Acids, bases and salts

trap.explanation: The slip: Acid sounds dangerous, so every acid is treated like it fully burns through everything. The fix: Weak acids only partly release their hydrogen ions: vinegar is still acidic, just not strong. In class, compare vinegar with a strong acid: both are acidic, but the weak acid has released only some of its hydrogen ions, so its pH is higher and it does not attack materials the way a strong acid does.

workedExample: Read the ladder, then neutralise. Step 1 (s2): the scale runs 0 to 14 and each step is ten times stronger, so a solution at pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one at pH 4 and one hundred times more acidic than one at pH 5. Step 2 (s4): neutralise hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide - the H+ and OH- ions pair up into water and the leftover sodium and chloride ions form sodium chloride, a chloride because the acid was hydrochloric. Check the ions: when the H+ and OH- counts are exactly equal, the mixture is neutral at pH 7.
